name: Bilal Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. We don't sell or campaign for anything. Your answers are confidential. What is an ordinary workday like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm usually the last person given a saw and the first asked to carry timber. At fifty-eight I'm still learning site carpentry; I left school early and came into building work late after years of warehouse shifts. My partner Nura packs lunch before I take the bus to the Brook Lane site. I like fitting a frame square, though my knees complain after a day hauling boards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew this is how building has always gone: someone buys a gadget and we still have to put up the walls. A few quicker measurements would be welcome, but I wouldn't call it a new age.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I need these ordinary wages more than I let on. Nura and I have about three months of bills saved, and I'm still the junior man at fifty-eight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll turn up at Brook Lane and keep learning the framing from Mateo, our foreman. In the first year I'd keep the same bus route and put the usual amount aside from each wage packet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly settled about the machines, though I am already watching the site calendar for gaps. One quiet fortnight would eat into savings faster than a clever app would help.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if the site calendar does have a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ring two contractors whose numbers Mateo gave me last spring. I wouldn't take a speculative course while there is a frame to finish and a wage coming in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say the technology is small, yet you keep mentioning your junior place. How do those fit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm not scared of the app itself; I'm scared of being the person a foreman can spare. A quiet site would hurt us with or without AI.

say: I'd tell the crew **walls** still need building, even if an app helps measure them.
I'd welcome **quicker measurements** if the work stays steady.
think: I need **ordinary wages** because our cushion covers about three months.
My **junior place** makes a quiet site more dangerous than a small software change.
do: Keep framing at **Brook Lane** and learn from foreman Mateo.
Set aside the **usual amount** from each wage packet.
feel: Mostly **settled**, with the existing site calendar still on my mind.
S0.quote: A quiet site would hurt us with or without AI.
fieldNote: Bilal speaks of tools with practiced scepticism, but his first private calculation is the household's **three-month reserve**.
His worry concerns being **junior at fifty-eight** and losing weeks on the site calendar, even under modest change.

steps.text: Keep framing at Brook Lane with foreman Mateo

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At lunch I'd say that software can order timber but it cannot hold a crooked stud while you fix it. I would ask why they aren't keeping younger apprentices when so many trades still need hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, fewer office staff could mean fewer jobs reaching the site, and nobody has promised our crew another contract. I can do the lifting, but I am slower than the fit men and still learning the finish work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask Mateo how long the Brook Lane contract lasts and keep going while the hours are there. If the firm starts cutting shifts, I'll take my handwritten list of contractors and ask about paid site work rather than gamble on a new machine course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel wary, like I do when the timber delivery doesn't arrive and nobody says why. I can act, but a lost month would take a real bite out of our savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of your work tasks could the software actually take?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It could do the material counts and the little schedule Mateo writes up. It cannot safely set the door frame I'm fitting, though a robot might do more later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say at home if shifts were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Nura the truth the same evening and stop the small weekend trips until hours came back. Our grown children have their own homes; I wouldn't quietly pass a bill to them.

say: I'd say **timber ordering** can change while site hands remain necessary.
I'd ask why firms aren't keeping **apprentices** for the work ahead.
think: I fear fewer office staff could mean **fewer contracts** reaching our crew.
I'm slower at **finish work** than fitter workers and cannot count on the next job.
do: Ask Mateo for the **contract end** date while keeping paid site hours.
Contact local **contractors** if shifts fall and pause weekend trips.
feel: **Wary** about lost hours, though I can still make calls.
S1.quote: Our grown children have their own homes; I wouldn't quietly pass a bill to them.
fieldNote: He separates material counts from the physical work he can still perform, then returns immediately to **contract continuity**.
His fallback is specific local contractors; he rejects speculative training and does not treat **adult children** as a financial plan.

steps.text: Ask Mateo when the Brook Lane contract ends
Contact listed contractors if site shifts are cut
Pause weekend trips if site shifts are cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the lads that a computer cannot carry today's timber, so we should finish the frame in front of us. I would also say a three-year wait for capable robots is not much comfort when you're nearing sixty.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At sixty, when the thinking system arrives, I could still earn on site if contracts survive. At sixty-three, when the robots arrive, I might be one of the first juniors taken off the rota; I haven't a pension amount I can safely live on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'll ask Nura to go through the monthly bills with me and set aside more from each paid week. In 2029, the first year after the 2028 thinking system, I'll stay on site if offered work and ask Mateo for hands-on tasks; if the rota starts thinning, I'll apply to the two local maintenance contractors on my list.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel a tightness in my chest about the rota, but I can still name my next steps. The speed makes me angry because it gives a learner of my age little room to prove himself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you reduce to save more now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nura and I would put the weekend bus trips and bought lunches on hold, perhaps forty a month. I would still pay for my knee check; pretending the pain is gone would cost me work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take early retirement when the robots came?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not without knowing what money would come in. At sixty-three I'd rather take repair jobs if anyone still needs a pair of hands.

say: I'd tell the crew to **finish today's frame** while hands are needed.
I'd say a **three-year wait** for site robots offers little comfort near sixty.
think: I could earn at **sixty** if site contracts survive the thinking system.
At **sixty-three**, robots may remove a junior from the rota before I can afford retirement.
do: Review **monthly bills** with Nura and save more from paid weeks.
Stay on site in **2029** and ask Mateo for hands-on tasks.
Apply to **maintenance contractors** if the site rota thins.
feel: **Tense and angry** about the speed, with a few concrete steps still available.
S2.quote: At sixty-three I'd rather take repair jobs if anyone still needs a pair of hands.
fieldNote: Bilal distinguishes a possible **site wage** at sixty from a much weaker position when hands-on robots arrive at sixty-three.
He will cut discretionary trips and save, but protects a **knee check** because health is part of staying employable.

steps.text: Set aside more from paid weeks after reviewing bills with Nura
Pause weekend bus trips and bought lunches
Keep taking site work in 2029 if offered
Apply to two maintenance contractors if the rota thins

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years gives a builder time to finish some jobs and see which machines actually work. I still wouldn't buy a promise from a salesman over what I can see on a site.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-three when the thinking system comes, and sixty-six when the robots could take the hands-on work. That gives us more pay packets, but I don't know whether retirement money will cover our rent and food then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'll keep my place on the site and put extra money aside when full weeks come through. In 2032, the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll keep taking carpentry shifts and ask Mateo whether repair calls are still paid; if those disappear by 2034, I'll ask our grown son whether he knows a small local builder hiring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel less cornered than in the fast picture, but not secure. My knees and the number of full weeks matter as much as the dates on that card.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ask your son rather than move to a new town?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He knows tradespeople here, and Nura's work and our home are here. I wouldn't move on the chance of a job someone has only mentioned.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you decide retirement is possible?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit with Nura and the actual figures after another couple of years of wages. Saying 'retire at sixty-six' without those figures would be a guess.

say: I'd say five years lets us **finish jobs** and watch what machines really do.
I'd refuse a salesman's **site promise** until I could see it working.
think: More **pay packets** may arrive before robots reach hands-on work at sixty-six.
I cannot claim **retirement income** will cover rent and food without the figures.
do: Keep **site shifts** and put extra money aside from full weeks.
Ask about paid **repair calls** in 2032 and local builders if those vanish.
feel: Less **cornered**, though my knees and uncertain workweeks still matter.
S3.quote: Saying 'retire at sixty-six' without those figures would be a guess.
fieldNote: **Extra years** make him more willing to build savings, but he refuses to assume a pension or a fixed retirement date.
His local network runs through an **adult son**; he sees no reason to move without a real offer.

steps.text: Put extra money aside after full site weeks
Keep taking carpentry shifts in 2032 if offered
Ask local builders about jobs if repair calls disappear

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is long enough to keep building while we decide our own future. If there are machines on sites in 2039, I expect the older workers will have left for different reasons as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be sixty-eight when the thinking system arrives and seventy-one when the robots come. I might have stopped paid site work by then, but I won't call that settled until Nura and I know the sums and my knees hold up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep showing up for current work and put money aside from full weeks rather than pay for a machine course I don't want. In 2037, the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'd still take safe paid repair work if I need it, and I would check our income and bills with Nura before deciding when to stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more room to breathe with ten years. The ordinary risks of weak knees and missed contracts haven't gone away just because the robot date is distant.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop site work before then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a doctor said the knees couldn't take ladders, I'd look for ground-level repairs first. Leaving wages altogether would depend on what Nura and I had saved by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the decade enough for your grown children to help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: They have lives and bills of their own. I'd rather give them a hand with a shelf than ask them to carry our living costs.

say: I'd say a **decade** gives us time to work and decide.
I'd expect some older workers to leave sites for **ordinary reasons** by 2039.
think: At **sixty-eight**, I may still need paid site work despite the thinking system.
I cannot settle **retirement** before Nura and I see our figures and my knees.
do: Keep taking current **site work** and save from full weeks.
Take safe **repair work** in 2037 if income is still needed.
Review **household bills** with Nura before deciding when to stop.
feel: More **breathing room**, while knees and missed contracts remain real worries.
S4.quote: I'd rather give them a hand with a shelf than ask them to carry our living costs.
fieldNote: The **distant robot date** eases his technology fear, yet his current junior status and physical strain keep money unsettled.
He would continue paid work if needed at sixty-eight and refuses to turn **grown children** into an assumed cushion.

steps.text: Keep taking paid carpentry work while fit
Put money aside after full workweeks

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because I could be losing site hours at sixty-three, before we know what living without my wage means. A clear contract calendar, honest notice of rota cuts and paid repair work nearby would help more than speeches about learning machines.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask how much pain people take to stay on a site. I'd pay for my knee check even if we cut the little trips, because without my legs I cannot offer the work I still know.

headlineQuote: I'm not scared of the app itself; I'm scared of being the person a foreman can spare.
portrait: Bilal is a **fifty-eight-year-old junior** site worker who came to carpentry late after warehouse shifts.
He and Nura have about **three months** of bills saved, making missed contracts a present worry.
He distrusts **unproven machines** and prefers paid framing and repair work to a speculative course.
Extra time lets him **save**, but he will not assume retirement income or support from grown children.
biggestWorry: The **2028 scenario** could remove his site hours when hands-on robots arrive around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: He wants an **honest contract calendar**, notice of rota cuts and paid local repair work.
